'''David Robert Nelson''' (born May 9, 1951) is an American [[physicist]],<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.physics.harvard.edu/people/facpages/nelson.html |title=Harvard Physics Department Faculty - David Nelson |website=www.physics.harvard.edu |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060104042518/http://www.physics.harvard.edu/people/facpages/nelson.html |archive-date=2006-01-04}}</ref> and Arthur K. Solomon Professor of Biophysics, at [[Harvard University]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.seas.harvard.edu/directory/nelson|title = Directory &#124; Harvard John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences}}</ref> He is known for developing [[KTHNY theory]].

==Education==

Nelson graduated from [[Cornell University]] ''Summa cum laude'' with a double major in physics and mathematics in 1972, and received an M.S. in theoretical physics in 1974, and a Ph.D. in theoretical physics in January, 1975. He was in the fourth and final class of Cornell's short-lived "Six-year Ph.D. program".<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://home.bway.net/lewis/phudbio.html#foury|title=Biographies of Students in the Six-Year PhD Program}}</ref> His thesis was on applications of [[renormalization]] to [[critical phenomena]], advised by [[Michael Fisher]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Nelson, David R., 1951- |url=https://history.aip.org/phn/11607019.html |access-date=2025-03-02 |website=history.aip.org}}</ref>

He then became a Junior Fellow in the Harvard Society of Fellows.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Listed by Term {{!}} Society of Fellows |url=https://socfell.fas.harvard.edu/listed-term-0 |access-date=2025-03-02 |website=socfell.fas.harvard.edu |language=en}}</ref>

Nelson is currently the Arthur K. Solomon Professor of Biophysics and Professor of Physics and Applied Physics at Harvard University.<ref>{{Cite web |title=David R. Nelson {{!}} Department of Physics |url=https://www.physics.harvard.edu/people/facpages/nelson |access-date=2025-03-02 |website=www.physics.harvard.edu |language=en}}</ref>

== Research ==
Since 1978 he has been a professor at [[Harvard University]]. His research is in the fields of both hard and soft theoretical [[condensed matter physics]], and of physical biology.<ref>{{Cite web |title=David R. Nelson {{!}} Department of Physics |url=https://www.physics.harvard.edu/people/facpages/nelson |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260218023601/https://www.physics.harvard.edu/people/facpages/nelson |archive-date=2026-02-18 |access-date=2026-05-19 |website=www.physics.harvard.edu |language=en}}</ref>

With his colleague, [[Bertrand Halperin]], he is responsible for a theory of two-dimensional melting that predicted a fourth [[hexatic phase]] of matter, interposed between the usual solid and liquid phases.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kosterlitz |first=John Michael |date=2017 |title=Nobel lecture: Topological defects and phase transitions |url=https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.89.040501 |journal=Reviews of Modern Physics |volume=89 |page=040501}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Brinkman |first=W.F. |last2=Fisher |first2=Daniel S. |last3=Moncton |first3=D.E. |date=1982 |title=Melting of two-dimensional solids. |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.217.4561.693 |journal=Science |volume=217 |issue=4561 |pages=693-700}}</ref> [[KTHNY theory]] is named after [[J. Michael Kosterlitz]], [[David Thouless|David J. Thouless]], Halperin and Nelson. A variety of predictions associated with this two-state freezing process have now been confirmed in experiments on two-dimensional colloidal assemblies, thin films and bulk smectic liquid crystals. Nelson's research also includes a theory of the structure and statistical mechanics of metallic glasses and investigations of tethered surfaces, which are two-dimensional generalizations of linear polymer chains<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kantor |first=Yacov |last2=Kardar |first2=Mehran |last3=Nelson |first3=David R. |date=1986-08-18 |title=Statistical Mechanics of Tethered Surfaces |url=https://journals.aps.org/prl/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevLett.57.791 |journal=Physical Review Letters |language=en-US |volume=57 |issue=7 |pages=791–794 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.57.791 |issn=0031-9007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250722194845/https://journals.aps.org/prl/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevLett.57.791 |archive-date=2025-07-22}}</ref>. Flexural phonons lead a remarkable low temperature flat phase in these fishnet-like structures, with predictions of strongly scale-dependent elastic constants such as the two-dimensional [[Young's modulus]] and the bending rigidity of atomically or molecularly thin materials such as a free-standing sheets of [[graphene]] and [[molybdenum disulfide]] (MoS<sub>2</sub>).

Nelson has also studied flux line entanglement in [[High-temperature superconductivity|high temperature superconductors]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Nelson |first=David R. |date=1988-05-09 |title=Vortex Entanglement in High- T c Superconductors |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevLett.60.1973 |journal=Physical Review Letters |language=en |volume=60 |issue=19 |pages=1973–1976 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.60.1973 |issn=0031-9007|url-access=subscription }}</ref>. At high magnetic fields, thermal fluctuations cause regular arrays of flux lines to melt into a tangled spaghetti state. The physics of this melted flux liquid resembles that of a directed polymer melt, and has important implications for both electrical transport and vortex pinning for many of the proposed applications of these new materials in strong magnetic fields. 
David Nelson's recent investigations have focused on problems that bridge the gap between the physical and biological sciences, including [[dislocation]] dynamics in bacterial [[cell wall]]s<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Amir |first=Ariel |last2=Nelson |first2=David R. |date=2012-06-19 |title=Dislocation-mediated growth of bacterial cell walls |url=https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1207105109 |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=109 |issue=25 |pages=9833–9838 |doi=10.1073/pnas.1207105109 |pmc=3382501 |pmid=22660931}}</ref>, range expansions and [[genetic demixing]] in microorganisms and localization in asymmetric sparse neural networks. Additional recent interests include the non-Hermitian transfer matrices that describe thermally excited vortices with columnar pins in Type II superconductors<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hatano |first=Naomichi |last2=Nelson |first2=David R. |date=1996-07-15 |title=Localization Transitions in Non-Hermitian Quantum Mechanics |url=https://journals.aps.org/prl/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevLett.77.570 |journal=Physical Review Letters |language=en-US |volume=77 |issue=3 |pages=570–573 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.77.570 |issn=0031-9007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260228073644/https://journals.aps.org/prl/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevLett.77.570 |archive-date=2026-02-28|arxiv=cond-mat/9603165 }}</ref>, the effect of perforations, cuts and other defects on atomically thin cantilevers at finite temperatures and topological defects on curved surfaces<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Moshe |first=Michael |last2=Esposito |first2=Edward |last3=Shankar |first3=Suraj |last4=Bircan |first4=Baris |last5=Cohen |first5=Itai |last6=Nelson |first6=David R. |last7=Bowick |first7=Mark J. |date=2019-01-28 |title=Nonlinear mechanics of thin frames |url=http://arxiv.org/abs/1801.08263 |journal=Physical Review E |volume=99 |issue=1 |article-number=013002 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevE.99.013002 |issn=2470-0045|arxiv=1801.08263 }}</ref>.
